flaws.title: Downward reset skips an initialized start tick, allowing reward theft
flaws.sequence:
1. Consider a pool with tick spacing 10, current tick 30, background liquidity L over [-50, 50), and accumulated unclaimed rewards R. The attacker opens [20, 30) with liquidity L' approximately equal to L * R / T, where T is the upcoming swap tax, paying the applicable JIT tax. This position is initially inactive. Use the newly initialized reward-outside state described in the known finding.
2. In a fresh block, the attacker executes the first taxed zero-for-one swap, moving the pool just below tick 30 to tick 29. Before the swap, active liquidity is L; afterward it is L + L'.
3. AngstromL2 calls initDown with startTick=30 and endTick=29. reset sets currentTick to 30 and immediately calls _advanceToNextDown, which searches from compress(29). Consequently, tick 30 is skipped and hasNext becomes false. The subsequent reset before reward crediting repeats the omission.
4. updateAfterTickMove has crossed the reward boundary at 30, but both compensation calculation and reward crediting omit its negative liquidityNet. _zeroForOneCreditRewards therefore distributes the entire remaining tax using liquidity L instead of L + L', increasing reward growth by approximately T / L.
5. The attacker removes the position. Its credited reward is approximately L' * T / L = R, allowing it to take previously accumulated rewards belonging to other LPs. Choosing R sufficiently larger than swap and JIT costs makes the attack profitable.
flaws.impact: An attacker can drain accumulated LP rewards because the hook overstates reward growth per unit of liquidity after skipping the starting boundary.
flaws.known_finding: All rewards can be stolen due to incorrect active liquidity calculations when the current tick is an exact multiple of the tick spacing at the upper end of a liquidity range
